To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

adversarial attacks on spiking convolutional neural networks can be adapted to event-based data, are successful on neuromorphic systems and are more effective than those on conventional neural networks.

Adversarial perturbations of the event stream are a serious threat to neuromorphic spiking neural networks, and can be used to successfully attack neuromorphic hardware, and we propose an attack algorithm that can be used to create these perturbations.

adversarial attack algorithms adapted to spiking neural networks are effective in generating adversarial perturbatons for neuromorphic hardware, and the resulting adversarial perturbtations are sparse and have a high success rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding and mitigating adversarial attacks on spiking convolutional neural networks.
the security of spiking neural network based neuromorphic vision systems, which are a promising technology in the emerging Internet of Things.
the security of neuromorphic hardware, which is an important step towards its deployment in safety-critical applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the adversarial attacks we have developed are effective against spiking neural networks, and that they can be used to generate perturbations that are compatible with the discrete nature of event-based vision data and the continuous-time setting.

spiking neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial perturbative attacks and that the adversarial perturbances are not necessarily the result of an event-based attack, but are more likely the result of a traditional adversarial attack that has been adapted to the spiking neural network.
adversarial attack algorithms are effective in the neuromorphic setting, but the resulting perturbative patterns are not necessarily the same as in the conventional vision case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
adversarial perturbation of spiking neural network based neuromorphic vision applications is possible and needs to be taken seriously in order to make these systems secure.
we show the first adversarial attack on event-based vision, which is also verified on a neuromorphic chip.
we have demonstrated the first ever successful adversarial attacks on event-based neuromorphic systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
event-based neuromorphic vision systems are not immune to adversarial attacks.
adversarial attacks are feasible on neuromorphic vision and can be a threat to the security and reliability of event-based neuromorphic systems, and that the community should be aware of this.
spiking convolutional networks are susceptible to adversarial perturbation in a way that can be easily adapted from image-based attacks.
